hypothesis.title: The Readable Constraint
hypothesis.question: Does preserving one named readability layer make a transformed passage feel more continuous than preserving surface similarity while breaking that layer?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a musical transformation preserves one named readability layer while changing surface features, then listeners will report stronger continuity than in a surface-matched control where that layer is broken.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: Low-frequency amplitude modulation can carry discriminative rhythmic identity in speech, suggesting that macro-temporal modulation may function as a readable rhythmic signature in music [S1]. Dynamic alignment between text and speech units improves prosody and stability in streaming synthesis, suggesting that timing alignment itself can be a task-relevant layer [S2]. ClariCodec shows that intelligibility can be optimized separately from acoustic reconstruction detail at 200 bps, so preserving the musically relevant message may matter more than preserving all surface fidelity [S3]. WST-X adds that multi-scale, deformation-stable features can retain subtle acoustic signatures under transformation [S4]. Ice-phase behavior warns that actual outcomes depend on reachable paths rather than all mathematically possible states [S5], while Tonnetz theory supplies explicit graph structures for preserving harmonic adjacency through variation [S6].

recipe.title: Preserve One Readability Layer
recipe.bodyMd: Build a 60-second piece from one four-bar source phrase containing drums, a monophonic lead, a chordal layer, and one noisy or synthetic timbral layer. Create four transformations plus one control. Keep BPM, form length, key center, integrated loudness, and source motif constant. Version A preserves the low-frequency amplitude-modulation profile: similar dominant pulse-rate region, dominant-peak count, and dispersion [S1]. Version B changes melody and accompaniment but keeps stressed events dynamically aligned to structural beat accents [S2]. Version C degrades timbre aggressively while protecting motif intelligibility, then compare it with a control that preserves more detail but obscures the motif [S3]. Version D revoices and reorchestrates harmony while preserving a reachable Tonnetz-like graph path through local plateau states [S5, S6]. The fifth version matches the surface palette but breaks the relevant constraints. The hypothesis is disconfirmed if listeners cannot identify stronger continuity in the preserved-constraint versions than in the broken-constraint control.

parameters.value: dominant AM peaks in ~1-10 Hz band

dawChecklist: Create one four-bar source phrase with drums, monophonic lead, chordal layer, and one noisy or synthetic timbral layer.
Duplicate it into five 60-second arrangements with the same BPM, form length, key center, motif, and integrated loudness.
For version A, alter drum samples and pattern surface while preserving the approximate low-frequency amplitude-modulation profile.
For version B, alter melody contour and accompaniment while keeping stressed events aligned to structural beat accents.
For version C, degrade timbre with filtering, bitcrushing, or resynthesis while keeping the motif easy to identify.
For version D, revoice and reorchestrate harmony while preserving one reachable Tonnetz-like adjacency path.
For the control, match the palette and energy but break modulation consistency, accent alignment, motif readability, and graph-path continuity.
Randomize exports and run a blind self-listening pass scoring continuity from 1 to 5 and naming what remains recognizable.

protocol.listeningContext: Level-matched headphones or nearfields; randomized export order.
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind continuity rating from 1 to 5 plus a short note naming the readable layer perceived.

notes: The control must be surface-matched enough that stronger continuity cannot be explained by simple loudness, density, or instrumentation similarity.
